title: Combine Two Tables
interviewTips: Ask if every Person must appear even without a matching Address - this distinguishes LEFT JOIN from INNER JOIN.
Clarify join key is Person.personId = Address.personId and what to do if one person has multiple addresses or none.
Trade-off: application-side nested loops vs DB LEFT JOIN - DB uses indexes and hash join and preserves NULLs automatically.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Nested-Loop Join
approaches.intuition: For each person scan all addresses to find a match, emitting NULLs when no match is found. This mimics a nested-loop join without an index and shows why INNER JOIN alone is wrong.
approaches.theory: Cartesian check of N persons x M addresses. If Address.personId equals Person.personId emit combined row, otherwise emit person with NULL city and state. Addresses with no person are ignored. This is logically equivalent to LEFT JOIN but costs O(N*M) comparisons.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of N persons scans up to M addresses for equality on personId, no index or hash used.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Stores one output row per person plus O(1) extra loop state.

dryRunExample.input: Person: (1, Allen, Wang), (2, Bob, Alice); Address: (1, 2, New York City, New York)
steps: p=1 Allen Wang scans Address 1: 2 != 1 so no match -> emit (Allen, Wang, null, null)
p=2 Bob Alice scans Address 1: 2 == 2 match -> emit (Bob, Alice, New York City, New York)
Address rows with no person are never emitted
dryRunExample.output: (Allen, Wang, null, null), (Bob, Alice, New York City, New York)

edgeCases: Person with no address must return null city and state, not be dropped
Address with personId not in Person is ignored
Empty Person returns empty result, empty Address returns all persons with nulls

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal LEFT JOIN
approaches.intuition: Let the database preserve all left rows. LEFT JOIN Person to Address on personId automatically keeps persons without addresses and fills city and state with NULL.
approaches.theory: LEFT OUTER JOIN is the relational operator for optional relationship. DB executes it via hash or indexed lookup in O(N+M) instead of nested loops. Equivalent application code builds a hash map from personId to address for O(1) lookup. INNER JOIN would incorrectly filter out persons without addresses.

timeComplexity.explanation: Hash map build over M addresses plus single pass over N persons; in SQL engine hash or index join gives same linear behavior.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Hash map of addresses by personId plus O(N) output; SQL itself needs only O(N) output.

dryRunExample.input: Person: (1, Allen, Wang), (2, Bob, Alice); Address: (1, 2, New York City, New York)
steps: Build map: {2 -> (New York City, New York)}
Lookup 2: hit -> (Bob, Alice, New York City, New York)
SQL LEFT JOIN does same preservation automatically
dryRunExample.output: (Allen, Wang, null, null), (Bob, Alice, New York City, New York)

edgeCases: Missing address yields NULL city and state via LEFT JOIN
Multiple addresses for same person yields multiple rows in pure SQL, first-row only in map version
NULL handling: do not use WHERE a.personId = p.personId after LEFT JOIN as it converts to INNER JOIN
